## Who this document is for

<span style="color:red">This document assumes a reader who administers the machines `{episomer}`
runs on: someone comfortable with a terminal, with Docker or Kubernetes, and with environment
variables.</span>

# Running episomer in containers

<span style="color:red">`{episomer}` ships with a `Dockerfile` and a `compose.yml` at the root of
its source repository. They are not published as a
ready-made image, so a deployment starts by building the image from the sources.</span>

## <span style="color:red">What the image contains</span>

<span style="color:red">The `Dockerfile` builds in three stages:</span>

-   <span style="color:red">**base** — a `rocker/r-base` image with the runtime prerequisites
    already installed: a Java 21 runtime, the system libraries the R dependencies need, and the
    LaTeX and pandoc installation the dashboard uses to export PDF and Markdown reports. A reader of
    the *Prerequisites* section of the main user documentation will recognise the list; in a
    container it is already done for you.</span>
-   <span style="color:red">**build** — adds the Java JDK and sbt, compiles the Scala code into the
    JAR that `{episomer}` embeds, installs the R dependencies and then `{episomer}` itself.</span>
-   <span style="color:red">**final** — the base image plus the installed R library. It runs as an
    unprivileged user (uid 1000 by default, configurable with the `EPISOMER_USER` build
    argument).</span>

<span style="color:red">One image serves every role. Which service a container runs is decided at
run time by the `EPISOMER_RUN` environment variable, read by the entry point:</span>

| <span style="color:red">`EPISOMER_RUN`</span> | <span style="color:red">What the container runs</span> |
|---|---|
| <span style="color:red">`FS`</span> | <span style="color:red">the episomer database, after a silent `setup()` that downloads and prepares everything missing</span> |
| <span style="color:red">`SEARCH`</span> | <span style="color:red">the post collection and processing loop</span> |
| <span style="color:red">`DETECT`</span> | <span style="color:red">the requirements and alert detection loop</span> |
| <span style="color:red">`APP`</span> | <span style="color:red">the full Shiny app</span> |
| <span style="color:red">`DASH`</span> | <span style="color:red">the Shiny app, dashboard page only</span> |
| <span style="color:red">`ADMIN`</span> | <span style="color:red">the Shiny app, admin pages only</span> |

<span style="color:red">A container started without `EPISOMER_RUN` says so and sleeps, rather than
guessing.</span>

## <span style="color:red">Configuring episomer through the environment</span>

<span style="color:red">A container has no interactive console, so the setup wizard cannot ask
anything. Everything it would ask is instead given through environment variables.</span>

### <span style="color:red">Where things live</span>

| <span style="color:red">Variable</span> | <span style="color:red">What it is</span> |
|---|---|
| <span style="color:red">`EPI_HOME`</span> | <span style="color:red">the data directory inside the container, i.e. what you would pass to `setup("data_dir")`. In `compose.yml` it is `/episomer-data`, backed by a volume.</span> |
| <span style="color:red">`EPI_HOST`</span> | <span style="color:red">the address of the episomer database, for every container that is not the database itself (`http://fs:8080` in `compose.yml`). See also *Running episomer on several machines*.</span> |
| <span style="color:red">`EPISOMER_INSTANCE`</span> | <span style="color:red">the name this container is known by in the logs and in the services status table. Always set it: a container host name is a random hexadecimal string.</span> |
| <span style="color:red">`EPISOMER_LOGS_TO_STDOUT`</span> | <span style="color:red">set it to `TRUE` in a container. `{episomer}` writes one log file per service under `<data directory>/jobs` by default, which is the right shape for a machine an operator logs into and the wrong one for a container: `docker logs` and `kubectl logs` read the standard output of the container and nothing else, so with the default the logs exist and are unreachable.</span> |

### <span style="color:red">Settings: `EPISOMER_OPTION_*`</span>

<span style="color:red">Any setting of `properties.json` can be given through the environment by
prefixing its name with `EPISOMER_OPTION_` and writing it in upper case. For instance
`EPISOMER_OPTION_RUNNER_TTL_SEARCH=600` sets the `runner_ttl_search` property, and
`EPISOMER_OPTION_SM_ACTIVATED_MASTODON=TRUE` activates Mastodon.</span>

<span style="color:red">Two things are worth knowing:</span>

-   <span style="color:red">**the precedence is defaults < `EPISOMER_OPTION_*` < `properties.json`.**
    An environment variable therefore only sets a property that `properties.json` does not already
    carry — which, since `{episomer}` saves every property when it saves its configuration, in
    practice means the very first start on a fresh data directory. On an existing data directory,
    edit `properties.json`.</span>
-   <span style="color:red">**values are typed and checked at startup.** A property whose default is
    a number must be given a number, one whose default is a boolean must be given a boolean
    (`TRUE`/`FALSE`, or `1`/`0`). An unusable value stops the container immediately, with a message
    naming the variable, rather than being discovered hours later in the middle of a loop.</span>

<span style="color:red">The social media of the deployment are set the same way, which is what
replaces option 6 of the wizard:</span>

| <span style="color:red">Variable</span> | <span style="color:red">What it does</span> |
|---|---|
| <span style="color:red">`EPISOMER_OPTION_SM_ACTIVATED_BLUESKY`</span> | <span style="color:red">whether posts are collected from Bluesky</span> |
| <span style="color:red">`EPISOMER_OPTION_SM_ALERTS_BLUESKY`</span> | <span style="color:red">whether Bluesky posts contribute to alert detection</span> |
| <span style="color:red">`EPISOMER_OPTION_SM_ACTIVATED_MASTODON`</span> | <span style="color:red">whether posts are collected from Mastodon</span> |
| <span style="color:red">`EPISOMER_OPTION_SM_ALERTS_MASTODON`</span> | <span style="color:red">whether Mastodon posts contribute to alert detection</span> |
| <span style="color:red">`EPISOMER_OPTION_MASTODON_INSTANCES`</span> | <span style="color:red">the Mastodon instances to collect from, separated by semicolons, e.g. `mastodon.social;mstdn.party`</span> |

### <span style="color:red">Credentials: `EPISOMER_SECRET_*`</span>

<span style="color:red">Credentials never go into `properties.json`; they are kept in an encrypted
keyring, and in a container that keyring is a password-protected file inside the data directory. Two
kinds of variables feed it:</span>

-   <span style="color:red">`EPISOMER_KR_PASSWORD`, the password that unlocks the keyring, or
    `EPISOMER_KR_PASSWORD_FILE`, the path of a file whose first line is that password. Without one
    of the two, a non-interactive `{episomer}` cannot open its keyring and stops with a message
    saying so.</span>
-   <span style="color:red">one `EPISOMER_SECRET_<NAME>` per credential, or
    `EPISOMER_SECRET_<NAME>_FILE` pointing at a file that contains it. The `_FILE` form is the one to
    use: it is what Docker secrets and Kubernetes secret mounts provide, and it keeps the value out
    of the container's environment, where `docker inspect` would show it.</span>

<span style="color:red">The names follow the social media:</span>

| <span style="color:red">Credential</span> | <span style="color:red">Variable</span> |
|---|---|
| <span style="color:red">Bluesky user</span> | <span style="color:red">`EPISOMER_SECRET_BLUESKY_USER`</span> |
| <span style="color:red">Bluesky password</span> | <span style="color:red">`EPISOMER_SECRET_BLUESKY_PASSWORD`</span> |
| <span style="color:red">Mastodon access token for one instance</span> | <span style="color:red">`EPISOMER_SECRET_MASTODON_<INSTANCE>_TOKEN`, where `<INSTANCE>` is the instance domain in upper case with its dots replaced by underscores — `mstdn.party` becomes `EPISOMER_SECRET_MASTODON_MSTDN_PARTY_TOKEN`</span> |

## <span style="color:red">The provided Docker Compose deployment</span>

<span style="color:red">`compose.yml`, at the root of the repository, starts the three services of a
working `{episomer}`:</span>

-   <span style="color:red">**`fs`** — the episomer database. It is the only service that holds data:
    the data directory is mounted into it as a volume, and it publishes the database port. Before
    starting the database it runs the setup wizard silently (`setup(silent = TRUE, launch =
    FALSE)`), which downloads and prepares whatever is missing — Java dependencies, GeoNames,
    language models — and then starts the database. The first start of a fresh data directory is
    therefore long.</span>
-   <span style="color:red">**`search`** — the post collection. It waits for `fs` to be healthy,
    talks to it over HTTP through `EPI_HOST`, and mounts only the `jobs` sub-directory. Its own
    health check asks `{episomer}` whether the social media authentication still works, so a
    container whose credentials have expired is reported as unhealthy rather than quietly collecting
    nothing.</span>
-   <span style="color:red">**`detect`** — the requirements and alert detection pipeline, with the
    same shape.</span>

<span style="color:red">`search` and `detect` are declared `restart: on-failure`, which is what makes
a container that cannot claim its lease — see the next part — retry until the lease is free, instead
of exiting for good.</span>

<span style="color:red">The `Makefile` wraps the whole thing, taking the credentials out of a `pass`
password store and handing them to Compose as secrets:</span>

```sh
make compose-up      # build the image if needed and start fs, search and detect
make compose-down    # stop them
```

<span style="color:red">If you do not use `pass`, export the `EPISOMER_KR_PASSWORD`,
`EPISOMER_SECRET_*` and `EPI_HOME` variables yourself and call `docker compose -f compose.yml up
--build -d` directly.</span>

<span style="color:red">Note that `compose.yml` starts no Shiny app: the three services above are
what a server deployment needs, and the app is expected to be run where the analysts are. To serve
it from a container as well, add a service using the same image with `EPISOMER_RUN` set to `APP`,
`DASH` or `ADMIN`, `EPI_HOST` pointing at `fs`, and its port published.</span>

## <span style="color:red">Two addresses, not one</span>

<span style="color:red">Two settings of `compose.yml` look redundant and are not, and a deployment
that changes one without the other will not work:</span>

-   <span style="color:red">`EPISOMER_OPTION_FS_URL` is the *interface the database binds*, not an
    address anything dials. It is a wildcard (`http://0.0.0.0`) because that is the one value that
    works unchanged under Docker and under Kubernetes, where a service name resolves to an address
    the container does not itself hold.</span>
-   <span style="color:red">`EPISOMER_OPTION_FS_SETUP_HOST` and `EPISOMER_OPTION_FS_SETUP_PORT` are
    where the *temporary* database of the language model retraining binds. They are deliberately as
    narrow as possible — loopback, on a port that is neither published nor routed — because while
    that retraining runs, the collection and the alert detection must **not** find a database, or
    they would start working against untrained language models.</span>

<span style="color:red">Opposite requirements, hence opposite values.</span>

# Running episomer on several machines

Everything described so far runs perfectly well on a single machine, and that is how `{episomer}` is
deployed almost everywhere. This section is about the other case: **one database, several machines**
— typically because the post collection has become too heavy for one host, or because you want a
second machine ready to take over when the first one is stopped for maintenance.

## The shape of a multi-machine deployment

There is exactly **one embedded database** (the `fs` service). It owns the Lucene indexes on its
local disk and it is the only process allowed to open them. Every other machine talks to it over
HTTP and holds no data of its own:

```
                    +--------------------------------------+
                    |  machine A        fs (the database)  |
                    |  Lucene indexes, runners/, *.json    |
                    +--------------------------------------+
                       ^                ^               ^
             HTTP      |                |               |     HTTP
       +---------------+                |               +----------------+
       |                                |                                |
+---------------+              +-----------------+             +------------------+
| machine B     |              | machine C       |             | machine D        |
| search loop   |              | search loop     |             | detect loop      |
| (collection)  |              | (standby)       |             | (alerts)         |
+---------------+              +-----------------+             +------------------+
```

Point every machine at the same database by setting `EPI_HOST` (or the `fs_url` / `fs_port`
properties) to the address of the machine running `fs`. A machine that is only a `search` or a
`detect` worker needs no data folder of its own beyond a scratch directory: `jobs/` for its logs and
a handful of small local files.

> The Shiny app is **not** a machine of that cluster. It reads and writes through the database like
> everything else, it never runs a collection loop, and several people may open it at the same time.

## One runner, one machine at a time

The problem a shared database creates is duplication. If two machines run the post collection for
Bluesky, both ask the API for the same posts and both store them — the alerts would then be computed
on doubled counts. `{episomer}` prevents this with **runner leases**.

A *runner* is a unit of work that only one machine may perform at a given moment:

| Runner | Held by | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `fs` | `fs_loop()` | the embedded database |
| `fs_mon` | the monitor started by `fs_loop()` | watches the database and beats for it |
| `search` | `search_loop()` | the parent of the collection service |
| `search.<network>` | one collection worker per social medium, e.g. `search.bluesky` | collects posts from that network |
| `detect` | `detect_loop()` | the <span style="color:red">alerts</span> pipeline |

A **lease** is the right, granted for a limited time and renewable, to be one of those runners. It is
one small JSON file per runner, stored on the database machine under `runners/`, and it works like a
key left on a hook:

* a service that starts **claims** the lease of its runner — it writes its identity in the file;
* while it works it **renews** it regularly, which only updates the file's modification time. This
  is the *heartbeat*;
* if the file has not been renewed for longer than its **time-to-live (TTL)**, the holder is presumed
  dead and another machine may take the runner over;
* a service that stops properly **releases** its lease, so the takeover is immediate rather than
  TTL-long;
* before every meaningful write — posting collected posts, saving `topics.json`, saving `tasks.json`,
  sending alert emails — a service **checks that it still holds its lease**, and exits cleanly if it
  does not.

A machine that cannot claim a lease does not start that runner. It says so in its log, naming the
machine that holds it:

```
Runner 'search.bluesky' is already held by another instance (7f3a1c2e) running on host
'machine-B' since 2026-08-28T09:14:02Z, last seen 12 seconds ago (lease TTL: 300 seconds).
This instance will not start it.
```

The exclusivity is per *runner*, not per service, which is what allows two useful setups:

* **standby** — machine C runs the same collection as machine B, fails to claim, and retries until
  machine B stops or disappears;
* **splitting the collection** — in principle machine B collects Bluesky while machine C collects
  Mastodon, since `search.bluesky` and `search.mastodon.<host>` are two independent leases. Be aware
  that this is *not* usable as it stands: `search_loop()` also claims the parent `search` lease
  before starting its workers, so the second machine is refused before it reaches them. This is a
  known and deliberate limit of the current release.

## Naming your machines: `EPISOMER_INSTANCE`

Every message and every status line about the leases names the machine that holds them, so give each
machine a name you will recognise:

```sh
export EPISOMER_INSTANCE="machine-B"
```

Without it `{episomer}` falls back on the host name, which inside a container is a random hexadecimal
string. Two machines must not share a value — not because it would be unsafe (`{episomer}` requires a
second, local proof before it declares a holder dead), but because you would not be able to tell
them apart in the logs or in the status table.

The name is *not* stored in the database: it describes the machine, not the deployment, and it is
read again at every start.

## Settings

Five properties tune the mechanism. They are stored in `properties.json`, which every machine reads,
so they belong to the whole cluster. They are **deliberately absent from the Shiny configuration
page**: a TTL mistyped there would break exclusivity for every machine at once, and these are
deployment knobs rather than analysis settings. Set them in `properties.json`, or through the
environment on a first deployment (`EPISOMER_OPTION_RUNNER_TTL_SEARCH=600` and so on<span style="color:red">; the precedence rule described in the section on `EPISOMER_OPTION_*` settings applies, so the environment only has the last word on a fresh data directory</span>).

| Property | Default | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `runner_heartbeat_span` | 30 s | time between two renewals |
| `runner_ttl_fs` | 120 s | TTL of the `fs` and `fs_mon` leases |
| `runner_ttl_search` | 300 s | TTL of `search` and `search.<network>` |
| `runner_ttl_detect` | 1800 s | TTL of `detect` |
| `runner_claim_guard` | 5 s | pause between claiming a lease and reading it back |

Two rules of thumb are worth keeping:

* **the TTL is your failover latency.** A machine that disappears without releasing anything — a
  crash, a cut network, `docker kill` — is replaced one TTL later, never sooner. Lowering a TTL to
  speed that up is the classic mistake: it makes healthy but busy services look dead, and *that*
  produces the duplication the whole mechanism exists to prevent;
* **keep the heartbeat roughly ten times shorter than the shortest TTL.** A few renewals lost in a
  row — a slow database, a network hiccup — must not be enough to expire a live lease.

`detect` has a much longer TTL than the others on purpose: one of its tasks (alert detection,
geolocation, aggregation) can legitimately run for a very long time without writing anything, and a
working service that looks dead is worse than a dead one noticed late.

## <span style="color:red">Watching a failover with Docker Compose</span>

<span style="color:red">The quickest way to see the mechanism at work is to start a second collection
container against the deployment of `compose.yml`, on the same laptop. Any container of the same
image with `EPISOMER_RUN=SEARCH`, the same `EPI_HOST` and a different `EPISOMER_INSTANCE` will
do:</span>

```sh
docker compose run --rm \
  -e EPISOMER_INSTANCE=search-standby \
  search
```

<span style="color:red">You will see the standby refuse to start, naming the container that holds the
lease, and retry — that retry loop *is* the standby, and it costs one read of one small file per
attempt. Then, from another terminal:</span>

```sh
docker compose stop search          # clean stop: leases released, takeover within seconds
docker compose kill search          # brutal stop: takeover after runner_ttl_search (300 s)
```

<span style="color:red">Watch the handover in the Shiny app, in the *Status* section of the
configuration page.</span>

# Operator guide: reading the runner leases {#leases}

## From the Shiny app

The configuration page shows<span style="color:red">, in its *Status* section,</span> a table with
one row per runner *currently holding a lease*, wherever in the cluster it runs:

| Runner | Status | Host | Last seen | Since |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| <span style="color:red">episomer database (`fs`)</span> | running | `machine-A (this machine)` | 4 s ago | 2026-08-28 07:02 UTC |
| <span style="color:red">Data collection & processing (`search.bluesky`)</span> | <span style="color:red">stale (no heartbeat for 8 min)</span> | `machine-B` | <span style="color:red">22 min ago</span> | 2026-08-28 07:05 UTC |
| <span style="color:red">Alerts (`detect`)</span> | crashed here | `machine-A (this machine)` | 3 min ago | 2026-08-28 06:58 UTC |

How to read it:

* **a runner with no row is free.** Releasing a lease removes its file, so "nothing holds it" and
  "it has never been started" look the same here — which is what you want. The table answers *who is
  holding what*, not *what could be started*; the Running/Stopped labels above it answer that.
* **`running`** — the holder renewed its lease less than one TTL ago. *Last seen* is the age of that
  renewal and should stay below `runner_heartbeat_span` most of the time.
* **`stale (no heartbeat for …)`** — nobody has renewed this lease for longer than its TTL. The
  holder is presumed dead and any machine may now take the runner over. It usually means the machine
  named in *Host* was stopped brutally, is unreachable, or has become too slow to renew. Look at that
  machine before doing anything else.
* **`crashed here`** — a stronger statement than `stale`, and a certainty rather than a presumption:
  the holder was a process of *this very machine* and the operating system says it is gone. It is
  reclaimable immediately, without waiting for the TTL. Restarting the service is the right move.
* **`Host`** is the `EPISOMER_INSTANCE` of the holder, with `(this machine)` appended when it is the
  machine you are reading the app from.
* **`Since`** is when this holder became the holder; it does not move when the lease is renewed.
  A long *Since* next to a short *Last seen* is exactly what a healthy runner looks like. It is shown
  in UTC so that it can be compared with the files and with the logs of the other machines.

<span style="color:red">Two runners are deliberately kept out of that table, because they are
internal plumbing rather than services a reader would recognise: `fs_mon`, the watchdog that keeps
the episomer database alive, which would read as a second database next to it; and `search`, the
parent lease of the collection. `search_loop()` claims `search` and then spends its life waiting for
its workers, with no iteration left to renew anything, so that lease goes stale a few minutes after a
perfectly healthy start. Its `search.<network>` children are the rows that say whether collection is
actually happening, and they are the rows to trust.</span>

## From the files

Everything the table shows comes from `<data folder>/runners/` on the database machine, and reading
it by hand is often the fastest way to understand a situation:

```sh
ls -l --time-style=full-iso runners/
cat runners/search.bluesky.json
```

```json
{
  "runner": "search.bluesky",
  "service": "search",
  "instance_id": "7f3a1c2e9b",
  "host": "machine-B",
  "pid": 41,
  "episomer_version": "4.0.5",
  "claimed_at": "2026-08-28T07:05:11Z",
  "renewed_at": "2026-08-28T07:05:11Z"
}
```

Three things are worth knowing before drawing conclusions from it:

1. **the freshness of a lease is the file's modification time, not anything inside the JSON.**
   `renewed_at` is only rewritten when the whole file is rewritten, i.e. when the lease is claimed —
   renewing merely touches the file. This is on purpose: the modification time is produced by the
   single machine hosting the database, so no clock difference between the other machines can make a
   dead lease look alive. Use `ls -l` (or the *Last seen* column), never `renewed_at`.
2. **`instance_id` changes at every restart, `host` does not.** `host` is the `EPISOMER_INSTANCE`
   value, i.e. the machine; `instance_id` identifies one *process*. Two lines with the same `host`
   and different `instance_id` are the same machine having restarted.
3. **`pid` is only meaningful on `host` itself**, and only when the two are read together — which is
   what lets a crashed runner be detected instantly on its own machine rather than one TTL later.

`runners/old/` holds the leases that were released, named `<runner>.<instance_id>.json`, with their
modification time as the release time. Nothing reads that folder; it is a trail left for you, and it
is the place to look to answer "when did that machine hand the collection over?".

## Common situations

| Symptom | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| A service refuses to start, naming another host | That machine holds the lease and is alive | Stop it there, or let it release the lease |
| Same, but naming *this* host | Another process of this machine is registered | The message names the PID to stop |
| A row stays `stale` and nothing takes over | No other machine is configured to run that runner | Start it somewhere, or restart the machine named in *Host* |
| A row is `stale` while the service is clearly working | The service is silent for longer than its TTL | Raise that TTL rather than lowering the heartbeat |
| The app shows a service as running while its machine is off | The lease has not expired yet | Wait for the TTL; it is the failover latency |
| `runners/` contains files but nothing is running | Services stopped without releasing | Normal after a crash; the files disappear when a new holder takes over |

Finally, a limit to keep in mind: the leases are **cooperative, not enforced**. They stop the
mistake, not a determined attacker — anyone who can reach the database can read, take or remove any
lease, exactly as they can read or remove any other file it serves. Protect the database machine at
the network level.
